newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Grain farmers want help in dry Europe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Grain farmers want help in dry Europe.

text.p: In the face of prolonged dry weather, Europe's grain farmers are starting to ask for help from government and the European Union.
But how much help there will be, and what form it will take is not yet clear.
EU structural fund measures have been used in the past to help drought-hit farmers, Gerard Kiely, spokesman for EU farm commissioner Franz Fischler, explained.
The EU had also used measures designed to make it easier for producers to switch to soya, after their wheat crops had been damaged by drought, he said.
"I expect it would be something along those lines," he said.
The immediate focus would be on helping farmers, rather than on the effect on the volume of grain produced. "It's too early to be looking at the effect of possible shortages of supply," Kiely said.
The commissioner had told EU agriculture ministers that their recommendations on farmers' aid needs would be looked at, he said.
Fischler told a ministers' meeting in Luxembourg on Tuesday that possible aid for Portuguese farmers would be studied.
France's Coordination Rurale farmers union asked President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday to provide aid for farms hit by drought.
It said the prolonged dry spell could prove disastrous for farmers, but that it was not seeking a special tax of the kind imposed in France during the serious drought of 1976.

"The lack of rain aggravated by drying winds and night frosts is progressively creating a drought situation that is becoming disastrous in many regions of France," union head Jacques Laigneau said in a letter to Chirac.

British farmers have not yet got to the stage of asking for aid to combat the drought, a spokeswoman for the England and Wales National Farmers' Union said. "At this stage it's too early to tell in this country," she said, noting that the main period for using irrigation on cereals had not yet started. "We can't see how bad the situation is yet," she said.
There is definite damage appearing on crops in eastern England, farming sources said. "Crops are starting to yellow," especially the late drilled ones," one co-op manager in eastern England said.
Scotland, however, is suffering from few of the drought worries seen elsewhere.
In France, the three month dry spell has irreversibly damaged durum wheat in the key production areas of the south, with regional analysts predicting losses of up to 40 pct.
In Spain, farming experts were expecting a soft wheat and barley crop of around one-third less than 1996's exceptional crop, after three days of rain ended months of dry weather.

Drought is less of a problem in central and eastern Europe. Unusually cold weather in Hungary this month will delay maize and potato planting and also put back wheat and barley growth by up to two weeks, the Hungarian Meteorological Office (OMSZ) said on Tuesday.
A Kazakh agriculture official said on Wednesday that dry weather would not hamper this year's grain crop and that rains were expected in May during sowing.

"We have seen higher than normal temperature levels this spring, causing problems with weeds," Nazarbek Kozhamsayitov, a weather analyst at the Agriculture Ministry, said. "But we expect rains in May."

In western Europe nature may solve, or at least help to lessen, farmers' problems. Light rains are expected to hit western France by Friday and more substantial precipitation may be in store for Saturday and Sunday, the national meteorological service Meteo France said on Wednesday.
And in England, there are definite signs of rain over the next few days, a spokesman for Britain's Meteorological Office said on Wednesday.
